o:
In a strictly increasing array, count triplets (i<j<k) with nums[j]-nums[i] = diff and nums[k]-nums[j] = diff, i.e., triples of values x, x+diff, x+2diff all present.

Example 1: 1,4,7 and 4,7,10 both exist with diff 3 → 2. Example 2: 4,6,8 and 5,7,9 with diff 2 → 2.

Constraints are tiny (n ≤ 200), so even brute force works; a hash set gives a clean O(n) solution.
k: The triplet condition is exactly: values x, x+diff, x+2diff all present in nums.
Strict increase guarantees uniqueness of indices for each value, so a set membership test suffices.

a.i: Put all values in a set; for each x count 1 if x+diff and x+2diff are also present.
s: Build a set of the array values.
For each element x, add 1 to the answer if both x+diff and x+2diff are in the set.
a.t: O(n) — one pass to build the set, one pass to count.

a.i: With n ≤ 200, checking all O(n³) index triples directly is perfectly acceptable and needs no extra insight.
s: Count triples where both differences equal diff.
a.t: O(n³) — three nested loops over ≤ 200 elements (≈ 1.3M checks).

w: Prefer the hash-set version — it generalizes to large inputs and is just as short. Because the array is strictly increasing, each value appears once, so set membership maps cleanly back to indices; on arrays with duplicates you'd need index-aware logic. Follow-up: count arithmetic subsequences of any length (LeetCode 1218-style DP on differences).
